newsitem.title: USA: TLC Beatrice PLC settlement on hold court.
newsitem.headline: TLC Beatrice PLC settlement on hold court.

text.p: A judge said he may need more information before ruling on a proposed $15 million plus interest settlement between closely-held TLC Beatrice International Holdings Inc and the estate of its late former chief executive Reginald Lewis.

The settlement is intended to resolve a 1995 shareholder lawsuit alleging fraud by Lewis and the company, which operates about 400 supermarkets in metropolitan Paris, France. The plaintiffs, Carlton Investments, want Lewis's estate to return to the company all of the $22.2 million he received in 1992 for managing the company in the preceding five years.

In a four hour hearing Wednesday before Chancellor William Allen of the Delaware Chancery Court, Carlton objected to the settlement, alleging that the bonus violated Lewis' compensation contract calling for a salary of $1 million a year, reasonable expenses, and a 50 percent equity ownership.

Allen said he would know next week whether "it may be necessary to have testimony from a member" of the independent board-appointed litigation committee before deciding whether the committee "knew enough about the strengths and weaknesses of the claims (of Carlton) to negotiate a fair and reasonable settlement."

Committee members include former FBI director William Webster and former Army Secretary Clifford Alexander. Among the Carlton principals are former Drexel Burnham Lambert senior executives Michael and Lowell Milken and Peter Ackerman. They acquired a 22.1 percent stake in Beatrice by floating junk bonds to help finance Lewis' $985 million leveraged buyout of Beatrice in 1987.
The attorney for Lewis's estate, Gregory Varallo, told Allen the settlement was "dictated" by the special committee, not negotiated.

"There was no liquidity in the estate so the settlement was the maximum that TLC could pay without losing control...My client was unwilling to go below effective control" which a TLC Beatrice attorney told Reuters was 51 percent.

But Carlton attorney Thomas Allingham asserted "If a settlement does not yield a maximum benefit to the company, then (it) should not be entered into...This settlement will not bring peace." But Allingham added that "if full recovery is achieved here, Carlton will not pursue" its pending lawsuit against Beatrice in a New York court alleging breach of contract.

TLC Beatrice chairwoman Loida Lewis, Reginald Lewis's widow, attended the hearing. Through a spokesman she said "I believe that this settlement is in the best interests of the company and its shareholders and we hope that it is approved."
